front.title: Start here · How to study with these cards
front.text: Every card has two sides. Front: one question and two or three cues for recall. Back: the answer, one structured box, the key point and the sources.

boxes.heading: Five steps
items: Read the question on the front.
Answer before you turn: in your head, aloud or in writing.
Rate yourself from 1 to 4: 1 didn't remember · 2 partially · 3 correct but unsure · 4 correct and confident.
Next time, review the cards you rated 1 or 2 first.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Answer before you turn. In controlled studies, recalling an answer led to better long-term retention than reading it again.

front.title: What is Periodontitis?
front.question: How is a clinical case of periodontitis defined in the 2017/2018 classification?
recall: Buccal/oral route: CAL and pocketing thresholds?

back.title: What is Periodontitis? — Answer
back.intro: Periodontitis is a chronic, multifactorial inflammatory disease associated with dysbiotic plaque biofilms, characterized by progressive destruction of the tooth-supporting apparatus. The case definition requires detectable CAL, not deep pockets alone.

boxes.heading: Case definition (either criterion)
items: Criterion 1: interdental CAL detectable at ≥ 2 non-adjacent teeth, OR
Criterion 2: buccal/oral CAL ≥ 3 mm with pocketing ≥ 3 mm at ≥ 2 teeth
Exclude CAL due to: traumatic recession
CAL on the distal aspect of a second molar, associated with malposition or extraction of a third molar
endodontic lesion draining through the marginal periodontium

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: PD alone does not define a periodontitis case.

references.text: Papapanou PN, Sanz M, Buduneli N, et al. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S162–S170. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12946
Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152

front.title: What is Periodontal Health?
front.question: How is periodontal health defined in the 2018 classification, and how do the criteria change after successful treatment of periodontitis?
recall: PD limit: intact vs treated periodontium
Does health erase the periodontitis history?

back.title: What is Periodontal Health? — Answer
back.intro: Periodontal health is defined by the absence of clinically detectable inflammation, with immune surveillance consistent with homeostasis. It can exist on an intact periodontium, on a reduced periodontium in a non-periodontitis patient, and in a successfully treated, stable periodontitis patient.

boxes.heading: Clinical criteria
items: Intact periodontium, or reduced periodontium in a non-periodontitis patient: BoP < 10% of sites
Successfully treated, stable periodontitis patient: BoP < 10%

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: A successfully treated periodontitis patient may present periodontal health on a reduced periodontium, but remains at increased risk of recurrence and must be closely monitored.

references.text: Chapple ILC, Mealey BL, Van Dyke TE, et al. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S68–S77. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12940

front.title: Plaque-Induced Gingivitis
front.question: What defines a plaque-induced gingivitis case in the 2018 classification, and how is its extent classified?
recall: PD, CAL and RBL on an intact periodontium

back.title: Plaque-Induced Gingivitis — Answer
back.intro: Gingival inflammation in response to dental biofilm. It may arise on an intact or a reduced periodontium, in a non-periodontitis patient or in a currently stable periodontitis patient. BoP % is the primary parameter that defines the case and its extent.

boxes.heading: Gingivitis case
items: Intact periodontium: BoP ≥ 10% · PD ≤ 3 mm · no CAL · no RBL
Reduced periodontium, no history of periodontitis: BoP ≥ 10% · PD ≤ 3 mm at all sites (excluding pseudopockets) · CAL may be present from non-periodontitis causes
Successfully treated stable periodontitis: BoP ≥ 10% with inflammation at shallow sites (PD ≤ 3 mm); no BoP-positive site with PD ≥ 4 mm; periodontitis history remains
Extent: localized BoP ≥ 10% and ≤ 30% · generalized BoP > 30%

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Plaque-induced gingivitis is reversible with effective biofilm control.

references.text: Trombelli L, Farina R, Silva CO, Tatakis DN. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S44–S67. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12939
Chapple ILC, Mealey BL, Van Dyke TE, et al. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S68–S77. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12940

front.title: Non-Plaque-Induced Gingival Diseases and Conditions
front.question: What are the 8 etiological categories of non-plaque-induced gingival diseases in the 2018 classification?
recall: What if the lesion persists after plaque control?

back.title: Non-Plaque-Induced Gingival Diseases and Conditions — Answer
back.intro: Pathologic gingival changes not caused by dental biofilm, often manifestations of systemic conditions or limited to the gingival tissues. Plaque accumulation may still influence their clinical course.

boxes.heading: The 8 etiological categories
items: a. Genetic / developmental — e.g. hereditary fibromatosis
b. Specific infections — bacterial, viral, fungal
c. Inflammatory / immune — lichen planus, pemphigoid
d. Reactive processes — e.g. pyogenic granuloma
e. Neoplasms — potentially malignant disorders and malignant neoplasms
f. Endocrine / nutritional / metabolic — e.g. vitamin C deficiency
g. Traumatic lesions — chemical, physical, thermal

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: A gingival lesion that does not resolve after adequate plaque control should not automatically be classified as plaque-induced gingivitis; investigate it according to the clinical presentation, with referral when appropriate. A clinically suspicious gingival or oral mucosal lesion requires prompt biopsy or specialist referral; do not wait for response to plaque control.

references.text: Holmstrup P, Plemons J, Meyle J. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S28–S43. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12938
Chapple ILC, Mealey BL, Van Dyke TE, et al. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S68–S77. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12940
Lingen MW, Abt E, Agrawal N, et al. J Am Dent Assoc. 2017;148(10):712–727.e10. doi:10.1016/j.adaj.2017.07.032

front.title: Clinical Attachment Loss (CAL)
front.question: What is clinical attachment loss, and how is it calculated?
recall: Formula in the three gingival-margin positions

back.title: Clinical Attachment Loss (CAL) — Answer
back.intro: CAL is the probing distance from the cemento-enamel junction (CEJ) to the apical extent of probe penetration. It provides a clinical estimate of periodontal attachment level using a fixed anatomical reference.

boxes.heading: How to calculate CAL
items: Gingival margin at the CEJ: CAL = PD
Gingival margin apical to the CEJ (recession): CAL = PD + recession
Gingival margin coronal to the CEJ: CAL = PD − coronal displacement

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: CAL is a central parameter for the diagnosis and longitudinal monitoring of periodontitis because it uses the CEJ as a fixed reference. It is a probing measurement, not a direct histologic one, and remains subject to measurement error.

references.text: Papapanou PN, Sanz M, Buduneli N, et al. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S162–S170. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12946
Listgarten MA. J Clin Periodontol. 1980;7(3):165–176. doi:10.1111/j.1600-051X.1980.tb01960.x

front.title: Probing Depth (PD)
front.question: What is probing depth, and how should it be measured?

back.title: Probing Depth (PD) — Answer
back.intro: PD is the distance from the gingival margin to the apical extent of probe penetration, measured with a calibrated periodontal probe.

boxes.heading: Measurement technique
items: Probe parallel to the root surface
Walking technique: small steps around the gingival margin
6 sites per tooth: mesio-buccal, buccal, disto-buccal, mesio-lingual, lingual, disto-lingual (palatal for upper teeth)

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: PD measures the probing depth of the sulcus or pocket, not attachment loss. It must always be interpreted together with CAL, BoP and RBL.

references.text: Chapple ILC, Mealey BL, Van Dyke TE, et al. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S68–S77. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12940
Scottish Dental Clinical Effectiveness Programme (SDCEP). Prevention and Treatment of Periodontal Diseases in Primary Care. 2nd ed. 2024.

front.title: Bleeding on Probing (BoP)
front.question: What does bleeding on probing tell us at patient level and at site level?

back.title: Bleeding on Probing (BoP) — Answer
back.intro: BoP is bleeding elicited from the gingival sulcus by gentle probing (0.20–0.25 N). At patient level, the percentage of sites with BoP measures the extent of inflammation: the thresholds for health (< 10%) and gingivitis (≥ 10%; localized ≤ 30%, generalized > 30%) apply together with PD and attachment loss.

boxes.heading: Predictive value (site level)
items: Lang et al. 1990, maintenance population of 41 treated patients followed for 2.5 years; bleeding sites re-instrumented; progression = attachment loss ≥ 2 mm

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Continuous absence of BoP at recall is a reliable indicator of periodontal stability, while its presence alone is a weak predictor. Smoking suppresses bleeding in a dose-dependent manner, so absence of BoP in a smoker must be interpreted with caution.

references.text: Chapple ILC, Mealey BL, Van Dyke TE, et al. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S68–S77. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12940
Lang NP, Adler R, Joss A, Nyman S. J Clin Periodontol. 1990;17(10):714–721. doi:10.1111/j.1600-051X.1990.tb01059.x
Dietrich T, Bernimoulin JP, Glynn RJ. J Periodontol. 2004;75(1):16–22. doi:10.1902/jop.2004.75.1.16

front.title: Radiographic Bone Loss (RBL)
front.question: What does radiographic bone loss measure, how is it expressed, and how is it used in staging?

back.title: Radiographic Bone Loss (RBL) — Answer
back.intro: RBL is the loss of alveolar bone support visible on intraoral radiographs, at the worst affected site, not attributable to non-periodontal causes. It is expressed as a percentage of root length.

boxes.heading: % RBL and staging
items: RBL (%) = [(CEJ–ABC) − 2 mm] ÷ [(CEJ–apex) − 2 mm] × 100 (ABC = alveolar bone crest; method: Fukuda et al. 2008)
Stage III–IV: extension to the middle third of the root and beyond

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Staging is primarily based on interdental CAL, with RBL as the substitute when CAL is unavailable. The 2018 classification expresses RBL as % of root length but does not prescribe a single measurement method. RBL alone does not assign the stage: tooth loss due to periodontitis and case complexity also count.

references.text: Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152
Fukuda CT, Carneiro SRS, Alves VTE, Pustiglioni FE, De Micheli G. Bull Tokyo Dent Coll. 2008;49(3):99–106. doi:10.2209/tdcpublication.49.99

front.title: Periodontal Probe Types
front.question: Which periodontal probe should be used for each clinical purpose?

back.title: Periodontal Probe Types — Answer
back.intro: Different probes serve different clinical purposes. The 2018 classification notes that lack of standardized probes, examiner variability and probing force limit the reliability of clinical criteria.

boxes.heading: Main types
items: UNC-15: millimetre markings from 1 to 15 mm — full periodontal charting
Williams: 1-2-3-5-7-8-9-10 mm (no 4 or 6) — routine clinical charting
WHO: 0.5-mm ball tip, black band 3.5–5.5 mm — population surveys (CPI) and patient screening (BPE, PSR), not full pocket charting
Florida Probe: force-controlled electronic system, force depends on device and version — standardized longitudinal measurement

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: For manual probing use a light, standardized force (about 0.20–0.25 N); force-controlled probes use device-specific preset forces.

references.text: Ainamo J, Barmes D, Beagrie G, Cutress T, Martin J, Sardo-Infirri J. Int Dent J. 1982;32(3):281–291.
Gibbs CH, Hirschfeld JW, Lee JG, et al. J Clin Periodontol. 1988;15(2):137–144. doi:10.1111/j.1600-051x.1988.tb01008.x
Chapple ILC, Mealey BL, Van Dyke TE, et al. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S68–S77. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12940

front.title: Gingivitis vs Periodontitis
front.question: What distinguishes gingivitis from periodontitis, and what can treatment achieve?

back.title: Gingivitis vs Periodontitis — Answer
back.intro: Gingivitis is inflammation in the gingival tissues; periodontitis adds destruction of the tooth-supporting tissues. Periodontitis is preceded by gingival inflammation in susceptible individuals, but not all gingivitis progresses to periodontitis. A periodontitis patient with gingival inflammation remains a periodontitis patient.

boxes.heading: Comparison (G = gingivitis, P = periodontitis)
items: Main lesion — G: inflammation in gingival tissues · P: inflammation + destruction of tooth-supporting tissues

CAL / RBL — G (no history of periodontitis): no periodontitis-related loss; support may be reduced for non-periodontitis reasons · P: periodontitis-related attachment / bone loss; the patient remains a periodontitis case after treatment
BoP — G: ≥ 10% of sites (with PD ≤ 3 mm and no periodontitis-related attachment loss) · P: may be present; does not define severity alone
PD — G: usually ≤ 3 mm (pseudopockets if enlargement) · P: may be increased
Outcome — G: reversible with biofilm control · P: lost attachment is not restored by biofilm control alone; the disease can be stabilized

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Managing gingivitis is a primary preventive strategy for periodontitis. Attachment lost to periodontitis is not restored by biofilm control, but periodontal health on a reduced periodontium and long-term stability can be achieved after successful treatment.

references.text: Chapple ILC, Mealey BL, Van Dyke TE, et al. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S68–S77. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12940
Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152
Chapple ILC, Van der Weijden F, Doerfer C, et al. J Clin Periodontol. 2015;42(Suppl 16):S71–S76. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12366

front.title: Concept of Stage
front.question: What does 'Stage' mean in the 2018 Classification, and how is the initial stage determined?

back.title: Concept of Stage — Answer
back.intro: Stage classifies periodontitis in 4 levels (I–IV) based on two dimensions: severity of damage and complexity of management.
intro_points: Stage I: initial periodontitis
Stage II: moderate periodontitis
Stage III: severe, risk of additional tooth loss
Stage IV: severe, risk of dentition loss, complex rehabilitation.

boxes.heading: How staging works
items: Step 1, initial stage by severity: interdental CAL at the worst affected site; if CAL is unavailable, RBL %; consider tooth loss due to periodontitis
Step 2, adjust upward with complexity: max PD, vertical bone loss, furcations II–III; tooth mobility, masticatory dysfunction; bite collapse, drifting, flaring
Complexity factors are evaluated collectively, not in isolation (Kornman & Papapanou 2020).

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: In successfully treated patients, CAL and RBL become the primary stage determinants. If a complexity factor is eliminated by treatment, the stage does not retrogress: the initial stage records the case's history and remains relevant for maintenance planning.

references.text: Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152
Kornman KS, Papapanou PN. J Periodontol. 2020;91(3):352–360. doi:10.1002/JPER.19-0557

front.title: Stage I Periodontitis
front.question: What are the diagnostic criteria for Stage I periodontitis, and what is its clinical significance?

back.title: Stage I Periodontitis — Answer
back.intro: Initial periodontitis: attachment loss has occurred but remains limited to the coronal third of the root. Clinically subtle, but periodontal destruction has occurred.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Stage I is the window of opportunity: damage is minimal and the case is amenable to control with effective biofilm management. Management typically follows Steps 1–2 of the EFP stepwise approach, with re-evaluation of the response over time.

references.text: Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152
Sanz M, Herrera D, Kebschull M, et al. J Clin Periodontol. 2020;47(Suppl 22):4–60. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13290

front.title: Stage II Periodontitis
front.question: What are the diagnostic criteria for Stage II periodontitis, and how does it differ from Stage I?

back.title: Stage II Periodontitis — Answer
back.intro: Moderate periodontitis: attachment loss reaches 3–4 mm, with bone loss still confined to the coronal third. Established disease, managed first with Steps 1–2 of the stepwise approach.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: The transition from Stage I to II marks established disease. Initial management follows the EFP stepwise approach: Step 1 addresses behaviour change, supragingival biofilm and risk-factor control; Step 2 adds professional subgingival instrumentation.

references.text: Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152
Sanz M, Herrera D, Kebschull M, et al. J Clin Periodontol. 2020;47(Suppl 22):4–60. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13290

front.title: Stage III Periodontitis
front.question: What are the diagnostic criteria for Stage III periodontitis, and what makes the management more complex than Stage II?

back.title: Stage III Periodontitis — Answer
back.intro: Severe periodontitis with potential for additional tooth loss. Damage extends to the middle third of the root or beyond, but masticatory function is preserved.

boxes.heading: Stage III criteria
items: Tooth loss due to periodontitis: ≤ 4 teeth
In addition to Stage II complexity, one or more of: maximum PD ≥ 6 mm; vertical bone loss ≥ 3 mm; furcation involvement Class II–III; moderate ridge defects
Masticatory function generally preserved; no Stage IV functional or rehabilitative complexity

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Stage III and Stage IV share the same CAL and RBL thresholds; Stage IV is set apart by 5 or more teeth lost to periodontitis, or by the need for complex rehabilitation because of Stage IV complexity features, evaluated collectively.

references.text: Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152
Kornman KS, Papapanou PN. J Periodontol. 2020;91(3):352–360. doi:10.1002/JPER.19-0557

front.title: Stage IV Periodontitis
front.question: What are the diagnostic criteria for Stage IV periodontitis, and what is the key clinical distinction from Stage III?
recall: Severity: CAL, RBL and tooth loss: ___
The two routes to Stage IV: ___

back.title: Stage IV Periodontitis — Answer
back.intro: Severe periodontitis with potential for loss of dentition and of masticatory function. Severity: interdental CAL ≥ 5 mm, RBL extending to the middle/apical third, tooth loss due to periodontitis ≥ 5. Stage IV may also be assigned when Stage III-level destruction is associated with major functional or rehabilitative complexity.

boxes.heading: Stage IV rehabilitative-complexity features
items: Need for complex rehabilitation of masticatory function

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Loss of 5 or more teeth to periodontitis establishes Stage IV severity; Stage IV is also assigned, with fewer teeth lost, when the case needs complex rehabilitation because of Stage IV complexity features. Neither route is the only one.

references.text: Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152
Kornman KS, Papapanou PN. J Periodontol. 2020;91(3):352–360. doi:10.1002/JPER.19-0557

front.title: Severity Criteria
front.question: What are the 3 parameters of severity used to determine the initial stage, and how do they map onto Stage I–IV?
recall: Primary parameter, and at which site: ___
Parameter used when CAL is unavailable: ___

back.title: Severity Criteria — Answer
back.intro: The severity dimension of staging quantifies how much periodontal support has been lost. Three parameters are used, in priority order: interdental CAL (primary, measured at the site of greatest loss); radiographic bone loss (% RBL), used when CAL is unavailable; tooth loss due to periodontitis, categorical, which may modify the stage.

boxes.heading: Severity mapping
items: Stage I: CAL 1–2 mm · RBL < 15% (coronal) · TL 0
Stage II: CAL 3–4 mm · RBL 15–33% (coronal) · TL 0
Stage III: CAL ≥ 5 mm · RBL mid/apical third · TL ≤ 4
Stage IV: CAL ≥ 5 mm · RBL mid/apical third · TL ≥ 5
TL = tooth loss due to periodontitis. Stage IV is also assigned with fewer teeth lost when Stage IV rehabilitative complexity is present.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Tooth loss due to periodontitis is a stage-modifying severity criterion and must be distinguished from tooth loss due to other causes. Severity is assigned from the site of greatest loss, not from the average.

references.text: Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152

front.title: Complexity Factors
front.question: What are the local and functional complexity factors used in the 2018 Classification, and how do they shift the stage upward?

back.title: Complexity Factors — Answer
back.intro: Complexity factors describe anticipated management difficulty. They may shift the final stage upward when the case is more difficult to treat than severity alone would suggest.

boxes.heading: Complexity by stage
items: Stage I: max PD ≤ 4 mm; mostly horizontal bone loss
Stage II: max PD ≤ 5 mm; mostly horizontal bone loss
Stage III, in addition to Stage II: PD ≥ 6 mm · vertical bone loss ≥ 3 mm · furcation involvement Class II–III · moderate ridge defects

Stage IV, in addition to Stage III, need for complex rehabilitation due to: masticatory dysfunction · secondary occlusal trauma (mobility ≥ 2) · severe ridge defects · bite collapse, drifting, flaring · < 20 remaining teeth (< 10 opposing pairs)

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Tonetti et al. (2018) write that, in general, one complexity factor may shift the diagnosis to a higher stage, giving Class II–III furcation involvement as the example. Kornman & Papapanou (2020) clarify that complexity factors are evaluated collectively, not in isolation: the question is whether the case as a whole requires more complex management. A single factor is a prompt to look, not an automatic upgrade.

references.text: Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152
Kornman KS, Papapanou PN. J Periodontol. 2020;91(3):352–360. doi:10.1002/JPER.19-0557

front.title: Extent & Distribution
front.question: How is the extent of periodontitis classified in the 2018 system, and what is the key change from the 1999 classification?

back.title: Extent & Distribution — Answer
back.intro: Extent describes the proportion of teeth involved. It is added as a descriptor to the stage diagnosis (e.g. 'Generalized Stage III'). In 1999 extent was based on % of sites; in 2018 it is based on % of teeth.

boxes.heading: The 3 categories
items: Molar/incisor pattern: breakdown affecting molars and incisors specifically
Sanz et al. (2020) clarify that extent is applied to the defined stage: the proportion of teeth involved at the stage-defining severity level.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Extent is a descriptor of the stage, not a modifier. A molar/incisor pattern should prompt careful assessment of age, rate of progression and grade.

references.text: Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152
Caton JG, Armitage G, Berglundh T, et al. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S1–S8. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12935
Sanz M, Papapanou PN, Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman K. J Periodontol. 2020;91(11):1385. doi:10.1002/JPER.20-0166

front.title: Tooth Loss due to Periodontitis (TLP)
front.question: How is tooth loss due to periodontitis used in the 2018 staging, and how should it be distinguished from other causes of tooth loss?
recall: Thresholds for Stage III and IV: ___

back.title: Tooth Loss due to Periodontitis (TLP) — Answer
back.intro: TLP is a severity-dimension parameter that may modify the stage, even in the absence of complexity factors. Count a tooth as TLP when periodontitis was the primary reason for its loss, including teeth extracted because they were periodontally hopeless. Do not count tooth loss whose primary cause was not periodontal (for example caries, endodontic failure, trauma, or orthodontic extraction).

boxes.heading: TLP staging thresholds
items: Stage I and II: no tooth loss due to periodontitis
Stage III: 1–4 teeth lost to periodontitis (0 is compatible with Stage III when CAL/RBL severity is Stage III)
Stage IV: ≥ 5 teeth lost to periodontitis — or fewer, when Stage IV rehabilitative complexity is present

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: A patient who has lost the most severely affected teeth may show lower CAL and RBL at the remaining teeth than the true disease history would suggest. Always establish why each tooth was lost, using history, records and radiographs, before assigning the stage.

references.text: Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152
Papapanou PN, Sanz M, Buduneli N, et al. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S162–S170. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12946

front.title: Common Staging Errors
front.question: What are the most frequent errors that students and clinicians make when applying the 2018 staging system to a periodontitis case?

back.title: Common Staging Errors — Answer
back.intro: A recent narrative review reports variable diagnostic accuracy with the 2018 system, with particular difficulty in distinguishing Stage III from IV and gingivitis from Stage I, in reporting hopeless teeth and in assigning extent.

boxes.heading: Six frequent errors
items: Using PD ≥ 6 mm alone to assign Stage III — stage starts from CAL, RBL and tooth-loss severity; PD ≥ 6 mm is a complexity factor and is interpreted together with the case as a whole, never alone
Counting all missing teeth as TLP — only teeth lost due to periodontitis count
Treating ≥ 5 teeth lost to periodontitis as the only route to Stage IV — five or more establish Stage IV severity; Stage IV rehabilitative complexity can establish it with fewer
Using site-based extent (1999 logic) — 2018 extent = % of teeth, not % of sites
Forgetting to add extent as a descriptor — a complete diagnosis includes extent, e.g. 'Generalized Stage III'
Using the average site instead of the worst — severity is assigned from the site of greatest loss

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Staging is a patient-level, multidimensional process. Check CAL at the site of greatest loss, cause-specific tooth loss, complexity factors and extent. Never stage on a single parameter alone.

front.title: Concept of Grade
front.question: What does 'Grade' mean in the 2018 Classification, what does it estimate, and what is the default starting grade before evidence?
recall: Primary criteria (2 types) and grade modifiers: ___

back.title: Concept of Grade — Answer
back.intro: Grading aims to indicate the rate of periodontitis progression, the responsiveness to standard therapy, and the potential impact on systemic health.
intro_points: Grade A: slow rate of progression
Grade B: moderate rate of progression
Grade C: rapid rate of progression.

boxes.heading: How grading works
items: Step 1, start by assuming Grade B: the default assumption in the absence of evidence; seek specific evidence to shift to Grade A or C
Step 2, apply the primary criteria: direct evidence, longitudinal CAL/RBL over 5 years; indirect evidence, % RBL ÷ age; whenever available, direct evidence should be used
Step 3, apply the grade modifiers: smoking and diabetes may shift the grade upward even when progression data suggest a lower grade.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Stage describes how much damage has occurred; grade estimates how fast it is progressing. Grade is assigned in addition to stage, at patient level: a low-stage case with evidence of rapid progression requires more intensive monitoring and risk-factor control than the stage alone would indicate.

references.text: Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152

front.title: Grade A
front.question: What are the diagnostic criteria for Grade A, and does heavy biofilm with minimal destruction alone justify assigning Grade A?

back.title: Grade A — Answer
back.intro: Grade A = slow rate of progression. It requires evidence supporting a slow rate; it is not the default grade.
intro_points: Direct evidence: no CAL/RBL loss over 5 years
Indirect evidence: % RBL ÷ age < 0.25

Case phenotype: heavy biofilm deposits with low levels of destruction. Heavy biofilm with little destruction supports a Grade A phenotype, but Grade A should not be assigned from phenotype alone: evaluate progression evidence and modifiers.

boxes.heading: Grade modifiers, Grade A row
items: A patient meeting Grade A progression criteria who smokes ≥ 10 cigarettes/day falls in the Grade C column of the modifier table.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Whenever available, direct evidence should be used. Grade modifiers may shift the grade upward because they indicate a higher likelihood of disease progression or a less predictable response to bacterial control.

references.text: Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152

front.title: Grade B
front.question: What are the criteria for Grade B, and why is it the default starting grade for periodontitis patients?

back.title: Grade B — Answer
back.intro: Grade B = moderate rate of progression.
intro_points: It is the assumed default:
clinicians start by assigning Grade B, then seek specific evidence to shift the case toward A or C. Direct evidence: CAL/RBL loss < 2 mm over 5 years (no loss corresponds to Grade A)
Indirect evidence: % RBL ÷ age = 0.25–1.0
Case phenotype: destruction commensurate with biofilm deposits.

boxes.heading: Grade modifiers, Grade B row
items: If risk factors reach the Grade C thresholds (≥ 10 cigarettes/day or HbA1c ≥ 7.0%), the case is shifted upward to Grade C.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Grade B is the starting hypothesis, not a definitive label. The clinical task is to confirm or move away from it using evidence. When evidence sufficient to shift the grade is lacking, Grade B remains the default assumption.

references.text: Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152

front.title: Grade C
front.question: What are the criteria for Grade C, and what clinical patterns suggest rapid progression even without longitudinal data?

back.title: Grade C — Answer
back.intro: Grade C = rapid rate of progression.
intro_points: Direct evidence: CAL/RBL loss ≥ 2 mm over 5 years
Indirect evidence: % RBL ÷ age > 1.0

Case phenotype: destruction exceeds expectations given biofilm deposits; specific clinical patterns suggestive of periods of rapid progression and/or early-onset disease (e.g. molar/incisor pattern; lack of expected response to standard bacterial control therapies). Response to therapy can only be assessed after treatment has been delivered.

boxes.heading: Grade modifiers, Grade C row
items: A modifier may shift a case to Grade C even when direct evidence of rapid progression is unavailable.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Grade C is assigned in addition to stage, at patient level. It indicates a case likely to progress faster or respond less predictably to standard therapy, and therefore to require more intensive prevention, monitoring and risk-factor control than the stage alone would indicate.

references.text: Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152

front.title: Direct vs Indirect Evidence
front.question: When grading periodontitis, what is the hierarchy between direct and indirect evidence, and what are the limitations of indirect evidence?
recall: Which one prevails, and its limitations: ___

back.title: Direct vs Indirect Evidence — Answer
back.intro: Grade assignment is based on primary criteria that document the rate of past progression. The 2018 framework ranks direct evidence above indirect evidence.
intro_points: Direct evidence: longitudinal radiographs or sequential CAL measurements; the thresholds refer to loss over 5 years; preferred when adequate longitudinal records are available; requires good-quality earlier records
Indirect evidence: % RBL ÷ age at the worst affected tooth; case phenotype (biofilm deposits vs destruction).

boxes.heading: Documented limitations of indirect evidence
items: Poor agreement with direct evidence in a retrospective cohort of 84 treated patients; indirect grading both overestimated and underestimated progression
Interpret indirect evidence as an estimate, not as equivalent to longitudinal evidence.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Whenever available, direct evidence should be used. Accuracy is nonetheless limited for both criteria: direct evidence is the framework's preferred option, not a perfect measure. When only indirect evidence exists, treat the grade as an estimate.

references.text: Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152
Bumm CV, Ern C, Folwaczny J, et al. Clin Oral Investig. 2024;28(5):289. doi:10.1007/s00784-024-05678-3

front.title: % Bone Loss / Age
front.question: How is the % bone loss ÷ age ratio calculated, and what are the grade thresholds for indirect evidence?

back.title: % Bone Loss / Age — Answer
back.intro: When longitudinal data are unavailable, grade is estimated indirectly by relating bone loss to the patient's age as a proxy for how fast the disease has progressed.
intro_points: Formula: % RBL ÷ patient's age (worst affected tooth). < 0.25 → Grade A (slow)
0.25–1.0 → Grade B (moderate)
> 1.0 → Grade C (rapid).

boxes.heading: Worked examples, same bone loss (50%)
items: Identical bone loss, different grades — age is the divisor.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Use the percentage of radiographic bone loss (not millimetres) at the worst affected tooth, and exclude bone loss from non-periodontal causes. The ratio is an estimate: whenever direct evidence is available, it should be used instead.

references.text: Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152

front.title: Case Phenotype
front.question: What does 'case phenotype' mean in grading, and how does the biofilm-vs-destruction relationship inform the grade?

back.title: Case Phenotype — Answer
back.intro: Case phenotype is a qualitative component of indirect evidence of progression that compares the observed periodontal destruction with the amount of biofilm present.
intro_points: Grade A: heavy biofilm deposits with low levels of destruction
Grade B: destruction commensurate with biofilm deposits
Grade C: destruction exceeds expectations given biofilm deposits.

boxes.heading: Use and documented limitation
items: Used together with the % RBL ÷ age ratio as indirect evidence of progression
A molar/incisor pattern is listed among the clinical patterns suggestive of periods of rapid progression and/or early-onset disease
Bumm et al. observe that the classification remains relatively vague on case phenotype: no exact quantifiable method is specified, so its comparability and usability can be considered low.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Case phenotype shifts the question from 'how much disease' to 'how much disease relative to the biofilm present'. It is a qualitative component of indirect evidence of progression, interpreted alongside the % RBL ÷ age ratio and the other grading criteria, not in isolation.

references.text: Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152

front.title: Smoking as Grade Modifier
front.question: How does smoking modify the periodontitis grade, what are the cigarette thresholds, and what are the clinical caveats?

back.title: Smoking as Grade Modifier — Answer
back.intro: Smoking is one of the two established grade modifiers, with diabetes. A modifier may shift the grade upward independently of the measured progression rate.
intro_points: Non-smoker → Grade A row
Smoker < 10 cigarettes/day → Grade B row
Smoker ≥ 10 cigarettes/day → Grade C row.

boxes.heading: Clinical caveats
items: Smoking suppresses the gingival bleeding response in a dose-dependent manner: BoP may be reduced despite active disease
Risk of periodontitis-related tooth loss decreases progressively after cessation.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Smoking is a modifiable risk factor. Risk-factor control, including smoking cessation, is part of the first step of the EFP stepwise approach to therapy.

front.title: Diabetes as Grade Modifier
front.question: How does diabetes modify the grade, what is the HbA1c threshold, and what is the bidirectional relationship between the two diseases?

back.title: Diabetes as Grade Modifier — Answer
back.intro: Diabetes is one of the two established grade modifiers. Glycaemic control, assessed by HbA1c, may shift the grade upward independently of the measured progression rate.
intro_points: Normoglycemic / no diagnosis of diabetes → Grade A row
HbA1c < 7.0% in patients with diabetes → Grade B row
HbA1c ≥ 7.0% in patients with diabetes → Grade C row.

boxes.heading: The bidirectional relationship
items: Diabetes → periodontitis: hyperglycaemia is associated with greater periodontal destruction
Periodontitis → diabetes: periodontal inflammation is associated with poorer glycaemic control

Effect of periodontal treatment: moderate-certainty evidence; periodontal treatment based on subgingival instrumentation reduced HbA1c by about 0.4 percentage points at 3–4 months compared with no treatment or usual care.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: The perio–diabetes link makes grading a communication tool with physicians. Given the established association between periodontitis and diabetes, coordinated medical–dental care is important, particularly when glycaemic control is suboptimal.

references.text: Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152

front.title: Common Grading Pitfalls
front.question: What are common pitfalls to avoid when applying the 2018 grading framework?
recall: mm vs %, and which tooth for RBL/age: ___

back.title: Common Grading Pitfalls — Answer
back.intro: A recent narrative review highlights difficulties and variability in applying the 2018 grading framework, particularly when longitudinal information is unavailable.

boxes.heading: Six common pitfalls
items: Not starting at Grade B — the default assumption is Grade B; shift only with evidence
Forgetting the grade modifiers — smoking and diabetes may shift the grade upward
Using mm instead of % — the RBL/age ratio uses percentage of root length, not millimetres
Using the wrong tooth for RBL/age — use the worst affected tooth, not an average or representative one
Over-trusting indirect evidence — the RBL/age ratio can over- or underestimate true progression
Confusing stage with grade — stage = severity and complexity; grade = rate of progression; grade is assigned in addition to stage, at patient level

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Grading is a structured sequence: assume Grade B, seek direct evidence, use the RBL/age ratio if direct evidence is unavailable, then apply the modifiers. Skipping steps can lead to incorrect grade assignment.

references.text: Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152

front.title: The Complete Diagnosis
front.question: How is a complete periodontal diagnosis assembled, and what are the 5 components of a full diagnostic statement?

back.title: The Complete Diagnosis — Answer
back.intro: Staging and grading do not make the diagnosis — they characterize it. First confirm periodontitis (interdental CAL at ≥ 2 non-adjacent teeth, or buccal/oral CAL ≥ 3 mm with pocketing ≥ 3 mm at ≥ 2 teeth, not attributable to non-periodontal causes), then build the full statement.

boxes.heading: The 5 components of the full diagnostic statement
items: Worked example: "Generalized periodontitis, Stage III, Grade B, BSP status: currently unstable; risk factor: current smoker < 10 cigarettes/day". The stable / unstable / in remission wording follows the BSP implementation (Dietrich et al. 2019).
Grade: A / B / C (rate of progression)
Status + risk: stable / unstable / in remission; smoking, diabetes

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: One patient = one stage + one grade. Confirm periodontitis first, then layer extent, stage, grade, status and risk factors. This single statement guides prognosis, treatment complexity and maintenance planning.

front.title: Localized Periodontitis
front.question: What does 'localized' mean as an extent descriptor, how is it calculated, and what is the common error to avoid?
recall: Localized threshold and unit (teeth or sites): ___

back.title: Localized Periodontitis — Answer
back.intro: 'Localized' is an extent descriptor indicating that fewer than 30% of teeth are involved. It is appended to the stage (e.g. 'Localized Stage III').
intro_points: Threshold: < 30% of teeth involved
Unit: % of teeth, not sites (key change from 1999)
Always exclude CAL from non-periodontal causes

Interpretative note: Sanz, Papapanou, Tonetti, Greenwell & Kornman (2020) clarify that extent is applied to the defined stage: it is the proportion of teeth involved at the stage-defining severity level.

boxes.heading: Common error
items: ✓ One extent + one stage + one grade
If regions differ in severity, the diagnosis takes the stage-defining level; the rest can be described in the narrative summary, not in the formal diagnosis.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Extent is expressed as a percentage of teeth present and is a descriptor of the stage: it refines the clinical picture but does not change the stage itself.

references.text: Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152

front.title: Generalized Periodontitis
front.question: What does 'generalized' mean as an extent descriptor, and how does it differ from 'localized' in clinical interpretation?
recall: Effect on stage and relationship to grade: ___

back.title: Generalized Periodontitis — Answer
back.intro: 'Generalized' is an extent descriptor indicating that 30% or more of teeth are involved.

boxes.heading: How to apply
items: The most severe site still determines the stage; extent describes how widespread the disease is.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Generalized does not mean 'more severe' — severity is captured by the stage. It means 'more widespread'. Widespread involvement should prompt assessment of risk factors and of the grade: a Generalized Stage II can coexist with risk factors that raise the grade.

references.text: Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152

front.title: Molar-Incisor Pattern
front.question: What is the molar-incisor pattern, what are its characteristic features, and how does it relate to grading?
recall: Relation to grading and role of age: ___

back.title: Molar-Incisor Pattern — Answer
back.intro: Molar-Incisor Pattern (MIP) is an extent descriptor for periodontitis concentrated around first molars and incisors.
intro_points: It captures a distribution previously often diagnosed as 'localized aggressive periodontitis'. Teeth: first molars and incisors specifically
Biofilm: often minimal relative to the severity of destruction
Usually systemically healthy patients
Familial aggregation frequently reported
Clinical association: often presents at an early age; however, age is not a defining criterion in the 2018 classification.

boxes.heading: Clinical significance
items: Destruction disproportionate to biofilm is a case-phenotype feature supporting a Grade C assessment
Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans has historically been strongly associated with this pattern
Adjunctive systemic antibiotics may be considered only in selected cases, in line with the EFP S3 guideline.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: MIP is a distribution descriptor, still diagnosed within the staging and grading system (e.g. 'Molar-incisor pattern periodontitis, Stage III, Grade C').

references.text: Tonetti MS, Greenwell H, Kornman KS. J Clin Periodontol. 2018;45(Suppl 20):S149–S161. doi:10.1111/jcpe.12945. Corrigendum: J Clin Periodontol. 2019;46(7):787. doi:10.1111/jcpe.13152

front.title: Periodontitis in Young Patients
front.question: How are young patients with severe, rapidly progressing periodontitis classified under the 2018 system, now that 'aggressive periodontitis' no longer exists?

back.title: Periodontitis in Young Patients — Answer
back.intro: The 2018 system abolished 'aggressive periodontitis' as a separate disease. Severe, fast-progressing disease in young patients is now diagnosed as periodontitis, then staged and graded.
intro_points: Distribution: may present as a molar-incisor pattern (MIP) — the phenotype once called 'localized / aggressive periodontitis'
Progression: rapid progression is captured by Grade C when the grading criteria are met
Diagnostic example: 'Molar-incisor pattern periodontitis, Stage III, Grade C'.

boxes.heading: Clinical clues (C-MIP)
items: : Onset usually before age 30, permanent dentition
A. actinomycetemcomitans, especially the JP2 genotype: a key association, not a diagnostic requirement.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Age is no longer a classification axis: the 2018 system describes rate of progression and susceptibility. What the old label tried to convey — rapid progression in a young patient — is now expressed by the grade, assigned from direct or indirect evidence of progression, of which the bone-loss/age ratio is one criterion.

front.title: Patients with Tooth Loss
front.question: How does tooth loss affect staging, and why did the 2018 system have to build it into severity explicitly?
recall: Counted tooth loss must be due to: ___
1–4 and ≥ 5 teeth lost to periodontitis → Stage ___

back.title: Patients with Tooth Loss — Answer
back.intro: CAL-based severity alone carries a paradox: losing the most affected teeth can make the remaining measurements look better. The 2018 system counts tooth loss attributable to periodontitis as part of severity. In a long-term retrospective cohort of treated patients, baseline Stage IV and Grade C were associated with significantly greater periodontitis-related tooth loss.

boxes.heading: Tooth loss as a severity criterion
items: Counts only if due to periodontitis (not caries, trauma, prosthetic or orthodontic causes)
1–4 teeth lost to periodontitis → at least Stage III severity
≥ 5 teeth lost to periodontitis → Stage IV severity (Stage IV can also follow from rehabilitative complexity)
It belongs to the severity dimension, not to the local complexity factors
The AAP FAQ specifies that tooth loss should include teeth planned for extraction due to periodontitis as part of active therapy.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: The clinical challenge is attribution: from history, records and radiographs, decide whether each missing tooth was lost to periodontitis or to another cause. Only periodontitis-attributable loss counts toward severity.

front.title: Borderline / Gray-Zone Cases
front.question: Before staging anything, how do you confirm a case is truly periodontitis — and what mimics it?
recall: Threshold: interdental CAL at ≥ ___ non-adjacent teeth, not attributable to ___

back.title: Borderline / Gray-Zone Cases — Answer
back.intro: A periodontitis case = detectable interdental CAL at ≥ 2 non-adjacent teeth, or buccal/oral CAL ≥ 3 mm with pocketing ≥ 3 mm at ≥ 2 teeth — not ascribable to non-periodontal causes.
intro_points: Reduced periodontium: stable periodontitis patient — treated; reduced periodontium; BoP < 10%; PD ≤ 4 mm; no BoP at 4-mm sites
Gingivitis on a reduced periodontium — BoP ≥ 10%, with no evidence of active periodontitis.

boxes.heading: Rule out these 5 (non-periodontal CAL)
items: Caries extending into the cervical area
Distal CAL of a 2nd molar (3rd-molar malposition or extraction)
Endodontic lesion draining through the marginal periodontium
These five are the exclusions listed in the case definition. Other sources of attachment loss exist clinically, but they are not part of that list.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: The case definition requires interdental CAL to be 'detectable' and does not set a numeric threshold for it, so borderline cases remain operator-dependent. BoP ≥ 10% flags inflammation operationally. When unsure, establish the cause of the attachment loss before staging and grading.

front.title: Differential Diagnosis
front.question: Once you've confirmed periodontitis, how do you decide which form it is — and which acute or systemic conditions must you tell apart?
recall: Papillary necrosis + pain/bleeding, with periodontal breakdown → ___

back.title: Differential Diagnosis — Answer
back.intro: After confirming periodontitis, identify the form. The 2018 system recognises three forms; the differential rests on history and specific signs.
intro_points: 1. Periodontitis — staged and graded (the common form)
2. Necrotizing periodontitis — papillary necrosis, pain and bleeding, with periodontal attachment and bone loss
3. Periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease — coded under the primary systemic disease.

boxes.heading: Also tell apart (not forms of periodontitis)
items: Gingivitis: inflammation without attachment loss due to periodontitis
Periodontal abscess: localized, rapid, with suppuration — an acute lesion
Endo-periodontal lesion: combined pulpal and periodontal involvement
Non-periodontal CAL: recession, caries, root fracture (see Card 37).

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: The differential rests on history and signs: necrosis and pain with attachment loss point to necrotizing periodontitis; an uncommon systemic disease altering the host response points to periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease. Most cases remain plain periodontitis, then staged and graded.

front.title: Diagnostic Checklist
front.question: What is the step-by-step sequence, from 'is this periodontitis?' to a complete diagnostic statement?
recall: Steps 1–2 — detect ___, exclude ___ causes, identify the ___

back.title: Diagnostic Checklist — Answer
back.intro: A reproducible diagnosis follows a fixed order. Staging and grading do not help you reach the diagnosis — periodontitis is confirmed first, then characterised.

boxes.heading: Step by step
items: Confirm periodontitis: interdental CAL at ≥ 2 non-adjacent teeth, or buccal/oral CAL ≥ 3 mm with pocketing ≥ 3 mm at ≥ 2 teeth; exclude non-periodontal causes
Identify the form (periodontitis / necrotizing / systemic manifestation)
Stage I–IV: severity (CAL, or RBL if CAL unavailable, at the site of greatest loss) plus tooth loss; complexity factors, evaluated collectively, may raise it
Grade A/B/C: rate of progression (direct evidence, or % bone loss / age) plus modifiers
Describe extent and distribution, current status and risk profile

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: The output is a single sentence — for example 'Generalized periodontitis, Stage III, Grade B, BSP status: currently unstable; risk factor: smoker'. Following the same order every time makes the diagnosis reproducible between clinicians.

Generalized interdental CAL 6–8 mm; deepest PD 8 mm; RBL to the middle third at several sites; 3 teeth lost to periodontitis; furcation at 2 molars; RBL%/age ≈ 1.2; BoP 35%. No Stage IV complexity signs are given: no < 20 remaining teeth, bite collapse, drifting/flaring, masticatory dysfunction or severe ridge defects.

back.title: Guided Clinical Case — Answer
back.intro: "Generalized periodontitis, Stage III, Grade C, BSP status: currently unstable; risk factor: smoking (~12 cigarettes/day)."

items: Confirm: interdental CAL at ≥ 2 non-adjacent teeth, or buccal/oral CAL ≥ 3 mm with pocketing ≥ 3 mm at ≥ 2 teeth, not ascribable to non-periodontal causes → periodontitis

Stage: interdental CAL ≥ 5 mm, RBL in the middle third → Stage III/IV severity; 3 teeth lost to periodontitis (1–4), no Stage IV rehabilitative-complexity features → Stage III

Extent/status: generalized; BSP status: pocket depths ≥ 5 mm with BoP → currently unstable

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: The reasoning matters: 3 teeth lost to periodontitis, with no Stage IV rehabilitative complexity, keeps it at Stage III; RBL%/age > 1.0 gives Grade C; smoking is a recognised modifier; BoP 35% with deep pockets makes it unstable. One stage, one grade, one sentence.

front.title: O'Leary Plaque Index
front.question: What does the O'Leary Plaque Control Record measure, how is it scored, and what is it used for?
recall: Result expressed as, and main clinical use: ___

back.title: O'Leary Plaque Index — Answer
back.intro: The O'Leary Plaque Control Record records the presence or absence of plaque on four surfaces of each tooth after disclosure, and expresses the result as a percentage of plaque-positive surfaces. It was designed to give the clinician a simple record of plaque on individual tooth surfaces, and lets the patient visualise their own progress in learning plaque control.

boxes.heading: How it works
items: Disclose plaque, then check each surface with a probe or explorer
4 surfaces per tooth: mesial, distal, facial/buccal, lingual/palatal
Occlusal and incisal surfaces are not scored
Dichotomous: plaque present or absent at the dentogingival junction

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: O'Leary is a disclosed, dichotomous plaque record converted into a percentage. It is well suited to patient motivation and follow-up, but it does not measure plaque thickness or gingival inflammation.

references.text: O'Leary TJ, Drake RB, Naylor JE. J Periodontol. 1972;43(1):38. doi:10.1902/jop.1972.43.1.38

front.title: Silness-Löe Plaque Index
front.question: How does the Silness & Löe Plaque Index differ from O'Leary, and what do its scores 0–3 represent?
recall: What it measures (plaque ___ at the gingival margin), and is disclosing needed?: ___

back.title: Silness-Löe Plaque Index — Answer
back.intro: The Silness & Löe Plaque Index grades plaque thickness at the gingival margin on a 0–3 ordinal scale. Teeth are dried and plaque is detected visually and/or with a probe, without routine disclosure.
intro_points: Per tooth = mean of its four surfaces; per patient = sum ÷ number of teeth
Designed as the companion of the Gingival Index (Löe & Silness 1963)
More an epidemiologic and research index than routine chairside charting.

boxes.heading: Scores 0–3 (thickness at gingival margin)
items: A film of plaque adhering to the free gingival margin, detected only with a probe or after disclosing solution
Moderate accumulation visible to the naked eye
Abundance of soft deposits at the gingival margin and/or within the sulcus

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Unlike O'Leary, Silness–Löe is not a yes/no percentage. It grades plaque thickness from 0 to 3; score 1 is the subtle one, detected only by running a probe along the gingival margin.

front.title: Bleeding Indices
front.question: What is the difference between dichotomous bleeding on probing and graded bleeding indices — and which BoP% thresholds matter in the 2018 framework?

back.title: Bleeding Indices — Answer
back.intro: Bleeding on probing is a simple, reproducible indicator of gingival inflammation. Indices differ in whether they record bleeding as present/absent or grade its severity.
intro_points: BoP / GBI (Ainamo & Bay 1975): presence or absence on gentle probing → % of bleeding sites
Gingival Index (Löe & Silness 1963): inflammation graded 0–3; bleeding on probing appears from score 2
Sulcus Bleeding Index (Mühlemann & Son 1971): graded sulcus bleeding.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Dichotomous BoP is the clinical workhorse and underpins the 2018 gingivitis thresholds. Graded indices add severity detail. In treated periodontitis patients, BoP must be interpreted together with residual pocket depth.

front.title: PSR (Screening & Recording)
front.question: What is PSR, what probe and codes does it use, and when does a code force a full periodontal charting?
recall: Code that always mandates full-mouth charting: ___

back.title: PSR (Screening & Recording) — Answer
back.intro: PSR (ADA and AAP, a modification of CPITN) is a rapid screen to decide who needs a full examination. WHO probe: 0.5 mm ball, coloured band 3.5–5.5 mm; six sextants; only the highest score per sextant is recorded.
intro_points: What to do:
0–2: preventive care
Code 3: charting of the affected sextant
Code 4: full-mouth periodontal examination and charting.

boxes.heading: Codes 0–4 (+ *)
items: Band fully visible (PD < 3.5 mm); no calculus or defective margins; no bleeding
Band fully visible; bleeding after probing; no calculus
Band fully visible; calculus or defective margins present
* = furcation, mobility, mucogingival problem, or recession reaching the coloured band — may be added to any code.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: PSR is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Record only the highest score per sextant. Code 4 always requires full-mouth charting; code 3 requires detailed charting of the affected sextant. PSR cannot stage or grade periodontitis.

references.text: Landry RG, Jean M. Int Dent J. 2002;52(1):35–40
American Academy of Periodontology, American Dental Association. Periodontal Screening and Recording (PSR). Chicago: AAP/ADA; 1992.

front.title: BPE (Basic Periodontal Exam)
front.question: How does the UK BPE differ from PSR, what do its codes mean, and what do codes 3 / 4 / * trigger?
recall: Probe band, and code 3 / code 4 probing depths: ___

back.title: BPE (Basic Periodontal Exam) — Answer
back.intro: The BPE (British Society of Periodontology, first developed in 1986) is the UK screening system: it indicates the level of further examination and basic treatment need, and does not provide a diagnosis. Same WHO probe and sextants as PSR; highest score per sextant.
intro_points: What to do:
0: no active treatment; 1–2: address bleeding and plaque-retentive factors
3: initial therapy including self-care advice and risk-factor control, then a 6-point pocket chart in that sextant only
4: 6-point pocket chart throughout the dentition
*: continue examining all sites in the sextant so furcations are not missed.

boxes.heading: Codes 0–4 (+ *)
items: No pockets > 3.5 mm; no calculus or overhangs; no bleeding (black band fully visible)
No pockets > 3.5 mm; no calculus or overhangs; bleeding after probing
No pockets > 3.5 mm; calculus or plaque-retentive factors present
Probing depth 3.5–5.5 mm (band partly visible; clinically a 4–5 mm pocket)
Probing depth > 5.5 mm (band disappears; clinically a pocket of 6 mm or more)
* denotes furcation involvement only, and is recorded together with the code (e.g. 3*).

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: BPE is a UK screening tool, not a diagnostic classification: it should be used for screening only. A code 3 may reflect a pseudopocket — confirm with full assessment before diagnosing periodontitis. BPE and PSR share the same band logic: code 4 when the coloured band disappears, i.e. probing depth > 5.5 mm.

front.title: CPI (WHO 2013)
front.question: What does the modified WHO Community Periodontal Index record, who is it for, and how does it differ from CPITN and from PSR/BPE?

Loss of attachment and calculus, compared with CPITN: ___

back.title: CPI (WHO 2013) — Answer
back.intro: The Community Periodontal Index is the WHO tool for population oral-health surveys. This card describes the modified CPI protocol of the WHO 2013 survey manual (Oral Health Surveys: Basic Methods, 5th ed.). It is not a diagnostic instrument for the individual patient.
intro_points: What it records:
gingival bleeding: 0 = absent, 1 = present
Periodontal pocket: 0 = absent, 1 = pocket 4–5 mm, 2 = pocket 6 mm or deeper
Recorded on all teeth present, with the WHO CPI probe (0.5 mm ball tip, black band 3.5–5.5 mm)
Loss of attachment is scored in a separate index on index teeth, by CEJ position, not within the CPI.

boxes.heading: CPITN → CPI → modified CPI
items: CPITN (Ainamo et al., 1982): hierarchical sextant codes 0–4 covering bleeding, calculus and pocketing, linked to treatment-need categories
CPI (WHO 1997): treatment-need categories no longer part of the index; loss of attachment recorded separately; calculus still recorded
Modified CPI (WHO 2013): calculus no longer recorded; gingival bleeding and periodontal pockets recorded as separate conditions; loss of attachment remains a separate recording
Published prevalence estimates may derive from different versions; always identify the recording protocol used.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: CPITN is the historical precursor of PSR and BPE: the three systems share related probe markings and pocket thresholds but differ in purpose and recording rules. None of them stages or grades periodontitis, and a CPI score is not a diagnosis for the person in the chair. When you read a prevalence figure, check which version of the index produced it.

front.title: Miller Tooth Mobility
front.question: How did Miller grade tooth mobility, and why do later “Miller” scales differ from one another?
recall: Tested by rocking the tooth between: ___

In the 2018 classification, mobility ≥ 2 acts as a ___ factor

back.title: Miller Tooth Mobility — Answer
back.intro: Clinical mobility is assessed by rocking the tooth between two rigid instrument handles and grading the amplitude of crown movement. The index most often cited is Miller’s; the 1950 edition of his textbook is used here as the historical source.
intro_points: Grade 1: first distinguishable sign of mobility greater than normal
Grade 2: crown movement up to approximately 1 mm from its normal position
Grade 3: movement of more than 1 mm and/or rotation or vertical depressibility
Charting baseline: Grade 0 = physiologic / no distinguishable mobility is used in many 0–3 renderings of the Miller index.

boxes.heading: Historical note
items: Later publications have reproduced or modified the Miller thresholds inconsistently, and clinicians were shown not to apply the original 1-mm reference reproducibly. Schemes such as “1–2 mm / more than 2 mm” are later modifications and should not be presented as the original Miller classification.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Mobility is a sign, not a diagnosis: it may reflect inflammation, reduced support or occlusal trauma. In the 2018 classification, tooth mobility of degree 2 or more counts among the Stage IV complexity factors (secondary occlusal trauma) — it can raise the stage, it does not define periodontitis.

front.title: Hamp Furcation Involvement
front.question: How does the Hamp system grade furcation involvement, and what exactly is it measuring?
recall: What is lost: ___ (attachment / periodontal tissue support)

back.title: Hamp Furcation Involvement — Answer
back.intro: Hamp, Nyman & Lindhe (1975) graded periodontal destruction in the furcation area by the horizontal loss of periodontal tissue support. The system describes the horizontal component only; it does not grade the vertical component. The 1975 paper describes loss of periodontal tissue support, not “attachment loss”. In the 2018 classification, furcation involvement Class II or III is a complexity factor that may raise the stage. Note the two vocabularies: Hamp uses degrees, the 2018 framework uses classes.

boxes.heading: The three degrees
items: Degree I: horizontal loss of periodontal tissue support less than 3 mm
Degree II: horizontal loss of support exceeding 3 mm, but not encompassing the total width of the furcation area
Degree III: horizontal “through-and-through” destruction of the periodontal tissue in the furcation
The original wording defines Degree I below 3 mm and Degree II above 3 mm. A value of exactly 3 mm is not assigned by the paper.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Hamp grades how far destruction extends horizontally between the roots: below 3 mm, beyond 3 mm but not through, or through-and-through. It says nothing about the vertical component, and it is not a diagnosis — in the 2018 classification, Class II or III furcation involvement acts as a complexity factor within staging.

front.title: Cairo Recession Types
front.question: How does the Cairo system classify gingival recession, and what does each type predict?
recall: Cairo is based on the ___ attachment level
RT1, RT2, RT3 (interproximal vs buccal loss): ___

back.title: Cairo Recession Types — Answer
back.intro: Cairo et al. (2011) proposed classifying gingival recession by the interproximal clinical attachment level. The 2018 World Workshop adopted the same three recession types in its case definitions for mucogingival conditions.
intro_points: RT1: gingival recession with no loss of interproximal attachment; the interproximal CEJ is clinically not detectable at either the mesial or the distal aspect of the tooth
RT2: interproximal attachment loss less than or equal to the buccal attachment loss
RT3: interproximal attachment loss greater than the buccal attachment loss
Interproximal loss is measured from the interproximal CEJ to the base of the interproximal sulcus or pocket; buccal loss from the buccal CEJ to the apical end of the buccal sulcus or pocket.

boxes.heading: What the type predicts
items: RT1 (Miller Class I and II): complete root coverage can be predicted
RT2 (overlapping Miller Class III): randomised trials indicate a limit of interdental attachment loss within which complete coverage remains predictable
RT3 (overlapping Miller Class IV): complete root coverage is not achievable

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Cairo classifies recession by interproximal attachment level relative to the buccal, and the type carries a prognosis for root coverage. Recording the recession type is therefore part of treatment planning, not merely a description of the defect.

references.text: Cairo F, Nieri M, Cincinelli S, Mervelt J, Pagliaro U. J Clin Periodontol. 2011;38(7):661–666. doi:10.1111/j.1600-051X.2011.01732.x

front.title: Common Index Errors
front.question: What are the most common mistakes when using and interpreting periodontal indices?

back.title: Common Index Errors — Answer
back.intro: Indices fail when their output type or their purpose is misread. Before recording a value, check what the index measures and what it was designed for.

boxes.heading: Don’t confuse these
items: Plaque output: O’Leary = percentage of plaque-positive surfaces; Silness–Löe = 0–3 score of plaque thickness at the gingival margin
Bleeding output: BoP / GBI = present or absent; Gingival Index = inflammation graded 0–3, with bleeding appearing from score 2
Screening ≠ diagnosis: PSR and BPE are screening tools that guide the need for further periodontal assessment; neither establishes the diagnosis, stage or grade of periodontitis
Furcation: Hamp grades the horizontal component only
Recession: Cairo is based on interproximal attachment level and carries a root-coverage prognosis
Code 3: a PSR or BPE code 3 is a screening finding, not a diagnosis of periodontitis; CAL, radiographic findings and the full case definition must be assessed before diagnosis
Extent: for periodontitis staging, extent is applied to the defined stage and is expressed by the proportion of teeth involved, not by the percentage of sites

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Before using an index, ask two questions: what does it output, and what was it designed for? A plaque percentage is not a thickness score; a yes/no bleeding record is not a graded index; a screening code is not a diagnosis. Indices inform the 2018 diagnosis — they do not replace it.

front.title: Clinical Case
front.question: Build a complete diagnosis. 30-year-old, systemically healthy, non-smoker. Interdental CAL 1–2 mm; fewer than 30% of teeth affected, none showing greater attachment loss. RBL ~12%, coronal third. Maximum PD 4 mm; no tooth lost to periodontitis. No vertical bone loss ≥ 3 mm, Class II/III furcation involvement, ridge defect or Stage IV rehabilitative-complexity features. Full-mouth BoP 20%, including bleeding at sites probing 4 mm.

back.title: Case: Stage I-B Localized — Answer
back.intro: Localized periodontitis, Stage I, Grade B; BSP status: currently unstable.

boxes.heading: Working it through
items: Confirm: interdental CAL at ≥ 2 non-adjacent teeth, or buccal/oral CAL ≥ 3 mm with pocketing ≥ 3 mm at ≥ 2 teeth, not ascribable to non-periodontal causes → periodontitis
Extent: fewer than 30% of teeth → localized
Stage: interdental CAL 1–2 mm, RBL coronal third (< 15%), no tooth loss due to periodontitis, maximum PD 4 mm, no Stage III/IV complexity factors → Stage I
Grade: no direct evidence of progression available; indirect evidence RBL % ÷ age = 12 / 30 ≈ 0.4 (0.25–1.0) → Grade B
BSP status: bleeding at sites probing 4 mm → currently unstable

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Stage I is the earliest detectable periodontitis: the interdental attachment loss is what separates it from gingivitis. Grade B is the starting assumption and is kept unless evidence shifts it. Status is a separate axis from stage — a Stage I case can be unstable.

front.title: Clinical Case
front.question: Build a complete diagnosis. 48-year-old, systemically healthy, non-smoker. Interdental CAL 3–4 mm at 30% or more of teeth, all at that level of severity. RBL ~25%, confined to the coronal third and predominantly horizontal; no Stage III/IV complexity features. Maximum PD 5 mm; no tooth lost to periodontitis. Full-mouth BoP 35%.

back.title: Case: Stage II-B Generalized — Answer
back.intro: Generalized periodontitis, Stage II, Grade B; BSP status: currently unstable.

boxes.heading: Working it through
items: Confirm: interdental CAL at ≥ 2 non-adjacent teeth, or buccal/oral CAL ≥ 3 mm with pocketing ≥ 3 mm at ≥ 2 teeth, not ascribable to non-periodontal causes → periodontitis
Extent: 30% or more of teeth → generalized
Stage: interdental CAL 3–4 mm, RBL 15–33% (coronal third), no tooth loss due to periodontitis, maximum PD 5 mm, mostly horizontal bone loss → Stage II
Grade: no direct evidence of progression available; indirect evidence RBL % ÷ age = 25 / 48 ≈ 0.5 (0.25–1.0) → Grade B
BSP status: pocket depth of 5 mm present → currently unstable

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Stage II is bounded by its own ceiling: CAL no more than 4 mm, bone loss within the coronal third, no tooth loss due to periodontitis, maximum PD 5 mm, mostly horizontal bone loss. Stage III severity findings — CAL ≥ 5 mm, RBL extending to the middle/apical third, or 1–4 teeth lost due to periodontitis — establish at least Stage III. Complexity factors such as PD ≥ 6 mm, vertical bone loss ≥ 3 mm and Class II/III furcation involvement must be evaluated collectively and may justify upstaging.

front.title: Clinical Case
front.question: Build a complete diagnosis. 42-year-old, systemically healthy, non-smoker. Interdental CAL ≥ 5 mm at 30% or more of teeth (worst site 6 mm). RBL ~55%, middle/apical third. Maximum PD 7 mm; vertical bone loss ≥ 3 mm; Class II furcation at one molar; 2 teeth lost to periodontitis; masticatory function preserved; no Stage IV rehabilitative-complexity features. Full-mouth BoP 45%.

back.title: Case: Stage III-C Generalized — Answer
back.intro: Generalized periodontitis, Stage III, Grade C; BSP status: currently unstable.

boxes.heading: Working it through
items: Confirm: interdental CAL at ≥ 2 non-adjacent teeth, or buccal/oral CAL ≥ 3 mm with pocketing ≥ 3 mm at ≥ 2 teeth, not ascribable to non-periodontal causes → periodontitis
Extent: 30% or more of teeth → generalized

Stage: interdental CAL ≥ 5 mm, RBL in the middle/apical third, 2 teeth lost to periodontitis (≤ 4), complexity factors present (PD ≥ 6 mm, vertical bone loss ≥ 3 mm, Class II furcation); masticatory function preserved and no Stage IV rehabilitative complexity → Stage III
Grade: no direct evidence of progression available; indirect evidence RBL % ÷ age = 55 / 42 ≈ 1.3 (> 1.0) → Grade C. No smoking or diabetes grade modifier applies
BSP status: pocket depths ≥ 5 mm present → currently unstable

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Stage III may include the loss of up to 4 teeth due to periodontitis when Stage IV rehabilitative-complexity features are absent. Stage IV can be assigned even with fewer than 5 periodontitis-related lost teeth when the case requires complex rehabilitation because of Stage IV complexity features. Grade C here rests on indirect evidence alone, a bone-loss/age ratio above 1.0; grade modifiers can raise a grade, they are not required to reach one.

front.title: Clinical Case
front.question: Build a complete diagnosis. 58-year-old, systemically healthy, non-smoker. Interdental CAL ≥ 5 mm at 30% or more of teeth (worst site 8 mm). RBL ~70%, apical third. 6 teeth lost to periodontitis; 18 remaining teeth; posterior bite collapse with drifting and flaring of the anterior teeth; tooth mobility degree 2; masticatory dysfunction. Full-mouth BoP 50%; pocket depths ≥ 5 mm present.

back.title: Case: Stage IV with Tooth Loss — Answer
back.intro: Generalized periodontitis, Stage IV, Grade C; BSP status: currently unstable.

boxes.heading: Working it through
items: Confirm: interdental CAL at ≥ 2 non-adjacent teeth, or buccal/oral CAL ≥ 3 mm with pocketing ≥ 3 mm at ≥ 2 teeth, not ascribable to non-periodontal causes → periodontitis
Extent: 30% or more of teeth → generalized

Stage: interdental CAL ≥ 5 mm, RBL in the apical third → Stage III/IV severity; 6 teeth lost to periodontitis (≥ 5) → Stage IV. The rehabilitative-complexity features present — bite collapse, drifting/flaring, mobility degree 2, fewer than 20 remaining teeth, masticatory dysfunction — collectively support the need for complex rehabilitation → Stage IV
Grade: no direct evidence of progression available; indirect evidence RBL % ÷ age = 70 / 58 ≈ 1.2 (> 1.0) → Grade C. No smoking or diabetes grade modifier applies
BSP status: pocket depths ≥ 5 mm with BoP → currently unstable

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: Stages III and IV share the same CAL and RBL thresholds; Stage IV is distinguished by greater periodontitis-related tooth loss and/or rehabilitative complexity, whose features are evaluated collectively. Here both routes are present. Stage IV is defined by the management the case requires, not by attachment loss alone.

back.title: Case: Smoker Patient — Answer
back.intro: Generalized periodontitis, Stage III, Grade C; BSP status: currently unstable; risk factor: smoking (15 cigarettes/day).

boxes.heading: Working it through
items: Confirm: interdental CAL at ≥ 2 non-adjacent teeth, or buccal/oral CAL ≥ 3 mm with pocketing ≥ 3 mm at ≥ 2 teeth, not ascribable to non-periodontal causes → periodontitis
Extent: 30% or more of teeth → generalized
Stage: interdental CAL 5 mm, RBL in the middle third, 1 tooth lost to periodontitis (≤ 4), PD 6 mm as a complexity factor; no Stage IV features → Stage III
Grade: no direct evidence of progression available; indirect evidence RBL % ÷ age = 40 / 46 ≈ 0.87 (0.25–1.0) → Grade B; grade modifier: current smoker ≥ 10 cigarettes/day → Grade C
BSP status: pocket depths ≥ 5 mm with BoP → currently unstable

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: The bone-loss/age ratio alone gives about 0.87, Grade B. Smoking of 10 or more cigarettes a day is a grade modifier and shifts the grade to C. Grade is first estimated from progression evidence and then adjusted upward when a risk-factor modifier indicates a higher grade. Smoking cessation becomes part of the plan.

front.question: Build a complete diagnosis. 15-year-old, systemically healthy, non-smoker, permanent dentition. Plaque and calculus minimal. back.title: Case: Adolescent, Molar-Incisor Pattern — Answer
back.intro: Molar-incisor pattern periodontitis, Stage III, Grade C; BSP status: currently unstable.

boxes.heading: Working it through
items: Confirm: interdental CAL at ≥ 2 non-adjacent teeth, or buccal/oral CAL ≥ 3 mm with pocketing ≥ 3 mm at ≥ 2 teeth, not ascribable to non-periodontal causes → periodontitis
Distribution: first molars and incisors → molar-incisor pattern
Stage: interdental CAL ≥ 5 mm, RBL extending beyond the coronal third, PD 7 mm as a complexity factor, no tooth loss due to periodontitis; no Stage IV features → Stage III
Grade: no direct evidence of progression available; indirect evidence RBL % ÷ age = 45 / 15 = 3.0 (> 1.0) → Grade C. No smoking or diabetes grade modifier applies
BSP status: pocket depths ≥ 5 mm with BoP → currently unstable

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: “Localized aggressive periodontitis” is no longer a separate diagnostic category. In the 2018 classification, molar-incisor pattern describes disease distribution; grade is assigned separately, from progression evidence. In this case, RBL % ÷ age = 3.0 supports Grade C. front.title: Clinical Case
front.question: Does this patient meet the periodontitis case definition, and what is the most likely diagnosis of the lesion at tooth 36? 39-year-old, systemically healthy, non-smoker. A single deep, narrow 10-mm pocket on the distal aspect of the mandibular first molar (36). The tooth is non-vital and tender to percussion, with a large periapical radiolucency tracking toward the furcation. No interdental CAL at ≥ 2 non-adjacent teeth and no buccal/oral CAL ≥ 3 mm with pocketing ≥ 3 mm at ≥ 2 teeth. Plaque moderate; full-mouth BoP 12%; no generalized bone loss.
recall: Is this a periodontitis case, and why not stage or grade?: ___

back.title: Case: Is It Periodontitis? — Answer
intro_points: Periodontitis case? No — not on the information given: neither arm of the case definition is met

Provisional diagnosis: endodontic-periodontal lesion in a non-periodontitis patient, tooth 36. Root damage, particularly vertical root fracture, must be excluded before the lesion is classified as “without root damage”
Essential assessment: pulp sensibility testing, percussion, periodontal probing with full charting, and appropriate radiographic evaluation; specifically assess for root damage
Do not stage or grade: staging and grading apply only after a periodontitis case is confirmed.

boxes.heading: Differential traps
items: Periodontal abscess: localized pus within the gingival wall of a pocket, rapid tissue destruction
Endo-periodontal lesion: non-vital pulp with a pulp–periodontal communication, deep narrow pocket
Vertical root fracture: isolated deep narrow pocket, often pain on biting
Localized periodontitis: requires the case definition to be met and non-periodontal causes of CAL to be excluded

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: The first question is not “What stage?” but “Is this a periodontitis case?” Here the provisional diagnosis is an endo-periodontal lesion at 36 in a patient who does not meet the case definition — so no staging or grading. CAL attributable to an endodontic lesion draining through the marginal periodontium, a vertical root fracture, or caries extending into the cervical area must be excluded before applying the periodontitis case definition.

front.question: Can you reconstruct the whole framework from memory — the Stage table and the three things that set the Grade?
recall: Stage is set by ___ (severity) + ___ (complexity); severity uses CAL, ___ and tooth loss
Grade is set by: rate of ___
Grade inputs: direct evidence, ___ /age, then risk ___

back.title: Staging & Grading at a Glance — Answer
back.intro: The whole system on one card: Stage by severity and complexity, Grade by rate of progression.
intro_points: Grade — direct evidence: CAL or RBL loss over 5 years — no loss = Grade A; < 2 mm = Grade B; ≥ 2 mm = Grade C
If unavailable: RBL % ÷ age — < 0.25 = A; 0.25–1.0 = B; > 1.0 = C
Risk-factor modifiers: current smoking < 10 cigarettes/day → Grade B modifier; ≥ 10/day → Grade C modifier. In patients with diabetes, HbA1c < 7.0% → Grade B modifier; ≥ 7.0% → Grade C modifier.

boxes.heading: Stage (interdental CAL · RBL · tooth loss due to periodontitis)
items: Complexity factors — PD ≥ 6 mm, vertical bone loss ≥ 3 mm, Class II/III furcation — are evaluated collectively and may raise the stage. Stage IV may also be assigned when Stage IV rehabilitative-complexity features collectively indicate the need for complex rehabilitation, even with fewer than 5 periodontitis-related teeth lost. Severity is scored at the worst affected tooth.

boxes.heading: KEY POINT
items: One patient = one stage + one grade. The diagnosis is a single sentence: [localized / generalized / molar-incisor pattern] periodontitis, Stage __, Grade __; BSP status: currently [stable / in remission / unstable]; risk factors. Confirm → form → stage → grade → extent and distribution → status.
